newsitem.title: TANZANIA: More Rwandan Hutu refugees in Tanzania flee - U.N..
newsitem.headline: More Rwandan Hutu refugees in Tanzania flee - U.N..

text.p: About 23,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees have fled camps in northwestern Tanzania in a growing exodus to avoid repatriation to Rwanda, U.N. officials said on Tuesday.
Tanzania sent a high-level delegation to the camps to explain why the 542,000 refugees must return to their tiny, ethnically divided central African country by a December 31 deadline.

U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) spokesman Peter Kessler said an additional 8,000 had followed 15,000 other Rwandan refugees who had abandoned their camps for the bush after Tanzania and UNHCR last week gave all refugees the order to return to Rwanda.
"The estimated 8,000 moved mainly yesterday (Monday)," he said. Aid workers in Tanzania said the refugees who left refused to discuss their destination.
But Kessler said a few other refugees were registering for repatriation and the UNHCR expected to transport some 800 back home on Tuesday.

In the northwest Tanzanian district of Ngara, another UNHCR official said the Interahamwe, Rwandan Hutu militiamen who led the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, had intensified their intimidation of the refugees.

The Interahamwe are determined not to go home because they fear reprisals for their role in the genocide of up to one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates in Rwanda in 1994. They fled when Tutsi guerrillas took power in Rwanda.

Anne Willem Byleveld, senior UNHCR official in Ngara, told Reuters refugees had fled in three directions, north, south and northeast. Most are illiterate peasants who believe they can make it to Kenya by foot.
"Between Friday and Saturday, the intimidators went house to house, door to door, telling the people to leave. It is very sad, the people are simply confused and lost," said Byleveld.
Byleveld said in one camp, the UNHCR had to remove a senior camp official who opposed the intimidators' tactics: "He was moved to safety. His life was threatened by the intimidators."

The exodus bodes ill for a repatriation plan for the 542,000 Rwandan refugees in Tanzania and it could end in bands of Rwandans wandering around the country, as happened in Zaire on the other side of Rwanda.
Last week's order by Tanzania and the UNHCR for refugees in 13 camps dotted around northwest Tanzania to return home has polarised the refugee population.

Some say they are willing to go back in large groups and others say they do not trust Rwanda's new government. Refugees interviewed by Reuters conceded many Tutsis were killed in Rwanda but denied there was an organised genocide.
Officials from the ministry of home affairs in the Tanzanian capital Dar es Salaam arrived in Ngara on Tuesday to win refugees over to the repatriation plan.

The Tanzania-UNHCR repatriation plan has been attacked by the London-based human rights group Amnesty International and the exiled Hutu lobby group Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy in Rwanda.
The two institutions accuse UNHCR of abandoning its principle of protecting refugees against forced repatriation. Tanzania has not said what will happen to those who refuse to return voluntarily.
